Thank you. Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished participants, good morning. Gender stereotypes are not abstract ideas. They shape how women are seen, heard, and judged every day, including in rooms like this one. Nearly nine in 10 people worldwide hold at least one bias against women, according to UN estimates. It's a stark reminder that gender stereotypes are neither marginal nor are they harmless. For many women, including myself, being judged on the basis of gender, scrutinized for appearances rather than work, and expected to conceal discomfort at sexist jokes remain everyday realities. People are placed into categories very early on. A sister who has to clean the house whilst her brother is doing homework. A boy bullied at work for being too humble. A migrant girl whose education is deprioritized because she is destined for other roles. According to UNICEF, girls aged 10 to 14 spend 50% more time on household chores than boys. When deeply entrenched stereotypes may seem normal or go unnoticed, they are often disguised as morality, family values, or established gender roles, and may even be presented as positive. But we should be under no illusion about their profound impact on human rights, primarily the rights of women and girls. Gender stereotypes fuel discrimination in insidious ways. poisoning our everyday practice, our institutions, and our laws. They are directly linked to exclusion, to violence, and a lack of access to economic opportunities and decision-making. And even where laws unlock many doors, stereotypes may still shackle women, preventing them from walking through. For women living at the intersection of multiple forms of discrimination and crises, these bonds tighten further. Biased media portrayals of LGBTIQ+ women can contribute to so-called corrective sexual violence against them. Negative stereotypes about parenting capacity of women with disabilities can result in forced contraception and sterilization. Gender stereotypes become particularly harmful during conflict and crisis, influencing who is targeted and how. silencing and stigmatizing victims, distorting investigations, and enabling impunity. From the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Myanmar to the occupied Palestinian territory, Sudan, Venezuela, UN investigative mechanisms have documented women being targeted as proxies to punish men and communities, while facing greater barriers to justice. Rape and gendered humiliation of men and boys were also used to assert power over the other warring party. Stereotypes can channel migrant women into informal work where they are at risk of exploitation and abuse. They also often shape attitudes in host communities. In Europe, for example, Muslim migrant women can be denied equal opportunities in workplace and politics in part because of harmful stereotypes. Stereotypes casting men as heads of households and economic decision makers also restrict women's access to land, to credit, to technology, and increasing their vulnerability to climate shocks. When women don't participate equally in the development of new technologies, human bias can be encoded into algorithms, and safeguards against online misogyny can be weakened. One study found that young men's TikTok and YouTube Shorts accounts began receiving manosphere content within 26 minutes of viewing. The cycle closes when all these violations and abuse become harder to challenge in courts, as stereotypes also influence who gets arrested, whose case is prioritized, and who is believed. Mr. President, let's stop calling these norms. Misogyny is not a norm. Patriarchy is not a value. Sexism is not a joke. These are harmful misconceptions, deliberately propagated for greater power and control over everyone. Beliefs about gender stereotypes shape our families, either around equality, freedom, and respect, or around domination and oppression. And that logic becomes the logic of our societies. It is no coincidence that the pushback against women's rights is unfolding alongside an autocratic resurgence and proliferation of violent conflict around the world. Last year, a study of 174 countries found that almost every country with low gender equality was an autocracy. We see this clearly in some of our current conflicts, where authorities are reinforcing stereotypes about women to tighten social control and, in some cases, to build support for militarization and nationalistic agendas. This pushback particularly targets politically active women and women human rights defenders who are seen as defying traditional gender norms. But this is not because gender equality doesn't work. It is precisely because it does. Attitudes that cherish freedom and equality help societies recognize injustice and challenge unchecked power. They make our commitments and our communities stronger. All around us, we see women mayors making cities safer and greener, women negotiators making peace agreements more durable, women leaders making institutions more responsive. And in my work, I have seen time and time again, women make a decisive difference in peacebuilding and in transitional justice. Excellencies, we need comprehensive strategies to remove corrosive bias from our institutions, our policies, and our systems. We need governments that invest in laws, in programs and advocacy to promote equal roles and share responsibilities and women's leadership. Embedding human rights in education and training at every level across all professions is a tried and tested way to foster dignity and respect across generations. We need employers that champion diversity and have zero tolerance for sexism. We need to turn technology from an amplifier of bias into a force for equality, using it to detect and eliminate discriminatory patterns. Understanding gender stereotypes is also essential for the effective administration of justice and law enforcement. This is why our office sponsors or supports governments around the world, from Cambodia to Costa Rica and Uruguay, in integrating a gender perspective into justice systems. Mr. President, when we fail women, we fail collectively as societies. When women advance, we all advance. So let's make equality the norm in how we think, in how we act, and in how we build our communities. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President of the Human Rights Council, Mr. Sidat Reza Suradipo, my own sister, Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, our double distinguished panelists, excellencies, colleagues, and friends. It's such an honor for me to be able to address the Human Rights Council on this agenda item. The United Nations Charter starts with we, the people. And it was with intentionality that Article 55 of the United Nations Charter embedded with clarity the issues around non-discrimination, including on the basis of gender, the discrimination of men and women. And indeed, the Bill of Rights is very clear on its emphasis that we are all born equal in dignity and in rights, and yet gender stereotypes do claw away on these fundamental, charter-rooted commitments. Gender stereotypes are at times dismissed as attitudes, as assumptions or matters of culture, but they are not harmless ideas. When they become embedded in laws, in policies, in institutions, in decision making, they shape what is protected and who is valued and who is punished and whose rights are negotiated. This is how stereotypes become structural discrimination. These stereotypes do not operate in isolation. They intersect with racism, with ageism, with ableism, I can attest to that as a woman living with disability, and other forms of discrimination, compounding exclusion for women and girls who face multiple overlapping inequalities. And this is why addressing them is simply a matter of changing individual attitudes. It is a matter of human rights and of structural transformation. 30 years of the Beijing Platform for Action, women still enjoy only 67% of the legal rights enjoyed by men and perform two and a half times much of the care work. These are issues that we know are embedded in the essence of CEDAW. This is why today's is so important. Integrating gender equality perspectives systematically across the Human Rights Council's work must mean more than counting women's participation. It must mean examining and transforming the laws, the institutions, the practices that produce unequal outcomes. UN Women's evidence shows that discriminatory norms and stereotypes are produced and reproduced through institutions that shape our lives, the state, the market, religion, community, and even the family. To dismantle them, we must change the rules, the incentives, and the structure that give those attitudes force. I always, also always reflect on the issue of language and how gender stereotypes are transmitted through language. For instance, what we call child marriage is under international law just rape. It's a crime in many of our jurisdictions. And yet, gender stereotypes reduce them to a social norm, to an articulation that rationalizes and normalizes a violation of human rights. UN Women's evidence also shows that stereotypes are produced very widely and very structurally. There are three mutually reinforcing pathways for doing so. First, we must transform the narratives. We must challenge the stories that present inequality as natural. as inevitable or beneficial and build broad support for equality and for human dignity. Yesterday, I had the opportunity to meet the first ever female Secretary-General of the Inter-Parliamentary Union. After 137 years, there's not been a woman elected to that role. And we know equally for WMO. took them 150 years. And we can count, including for ourselves in the United Nations, where we have only had five women as presidents of the General Assembly. And we are yet to even say good morning, Madam Secretary General. All this is embedded in the notion and the stereotype around women as leaders and as decision makers. Therefore, it is important to change the material conditions. A woman cannot overcome a stereotype about her economic role if the law restricts her access to employment or assets. A girl cannot overcome expectation of care if she's required to leave school or care for her family. And women cannot achieve equality in the workplace if unpaid care remains undistributed. We must move from just formal equality, which is important, to substantive equality, within which gender stereotype undermines that possibility. Third, it's important to strengthen the power and voice of those advocating for change. Women's organizations, feminist movements, people facing intersecting discrimination are not just beneficiaries, they are agents of change and need resources, protection and political space that shape the laws, the policies and the institutions. This is why the work of this Human Rights Council is very important and is over time looked at protecting human rights defenders who at times really lived on these issues. A key stereotype about women is that they don't work. Rooted in the norms that cast men as breadwinners and women as homemakers, this stereotype persists despite women's visible contribution in homes, on farms, factories, on the streets, in public and in private sector. Therefore, we call on the Council and States to take the following concrete steps. First, eliminate gender stereotypes in laws, judicial reasoning, in public policy and institutional practice. Second, Integrate gender stereotype analysis systematically across the universal periodic review, special procedures, investigations, and council resolutions. Third, establish effective training, oversight, and complaints procedures and remedies where stereotypes influence decision by judges, prosecutors, the police, health professionals, and other public officials. It is important to equally strengthen the role of independent national human rights mechanisms, as they also play a critical role. Fourth, assess artificial intelligence and algorithmic systems for bias and discrimination and discriminatory outcomes. We are pleased to see that in the recently concluded high-level week of the UN General Assembly, there was a strong, strong call on global AI governance, and for us, this also relates to technology technology-facilitated violence. Finally, resource, fund and protect women's organizations in the affected communities as leaders in the design, implementation and monitoring of reform. As we heard at the CSW70, formal equality before the law is not enough if stereotypes determine whose testimony is credible and whose harm is recognized and who can obtain an effective remedy. UN Women stands ready to support states in the Human Rights Council and its mechanisms in translating international recommendations into country level reform. We will continue to work with the CEDAW Committee, with the Working Group on Non-Discrimination, with indeed the Office of the High Commissioner, including in relation to the forthcoming General Recommendation No. 41 on dismantling gender stereotypes. We are as UN Women also proud to support you, Mr. President, with your Advisory Board on Gender Equality, the board for which we are honored to serve and which brings member states, partners and human rights mechanisms together with civil society to action some of these issues on inequality systematically embedded through the Council's work. We cannot dismantle structural discrimination while leaving intact the ideologies, institutions and relations that sustain it. We therefore look forward to carrying through this discussion through the UN Commission on the Status of Women 71, which would be focusing on the SDGs, and to carry forward those commitments in our ongoing work and in our communities and with the countries that we serve. Again, thank you so much, Mr. President.

Good morning. The CERD Committee is pleased to have this opportunity to address you here today. The CERD Convention was adopted in 1979. and the committee met for the first time in 1982. This committee is mandated by Article 21 of its convention on the elimination of all forms of discrimination against women to develop general recommendations with the aim of providing authoritative guidance to states parties on legislative policy and other appropriate measures to ensure the implementation of the obligations under the conventions. So I welcome all the States Parties who are present. Since its inception, general recommendations have been developed by CEDAW and become more comprehensive over the years. GR 41, General Recommendation 41 on dismantling gender stereotypes, prejudices and stigma and the power relations that sustain them is our latest general recommendation. It interprets and develops upon Article 5A of the Convention, which calls on States Parties, and I quote, "to modify the social and cultural patterns of conduct of men and women with a view to achieving the elimination of prejudices and customary and all other practices based on the idea of the inferiority or superiority of either of the sexes or on stereotyped rules for men and women. I always say that this is one of the most important articles because it identifies the basis for the other discriminatory practices that women experience. This general recommendation provides a more in-depth interpretation of the scope and nature of States Parties' obligations under Article 5 and Article 10C to address gender stereotyping as a form of discrimination against women. It provides guidance to States Parties on legislative policy and other relevant measures to ensure the implementation of their obligations under the Convention. Article 5 is the only article that specifically mentions men and boys, providing the opportunity to address how men and boys are affected. Gender stereotypes are often rooted, as we have heard on this distinguished panel already, in notions of women and girls' inferiority and lesser value, and the assumed value and superiority of men and boys. They normalize and legitimize women and girls' unequal worth, inequality and subordination from birth. They are embedded in everyday behaviors, rules and standards in institutions such as the state, economy, labor market, community, religious institutions and the family. Gender stereotypes justify existing discriminatory behaviors, the norms, rules, and practices that determine the roles, power, and privileges of men and women in these institutions. Dismantling gender stereotypes, therefore, requires the transformation of discriminatory ideas and rules and standards that support them in all areas of life, and addressing the stigma affecting many special groups faced by intersectional discrimination. Intersectional discrimination is the result of intersecting axes and systems of inequality. Although, sorry, for example, racism, casteism, colorism, sex and gender-based discrimination, ageism, ableism, and class inequality. So although they are often perceived as separate axes within the social structure and in everyday practice, they simultaneously interact with each other to shape women's and men's lives. Those axes are connected to broader systems of oppression. including political, colonial, and patriarchal structures, which reinforce each other. One innovation of this GR is the location of gender stereotypes within these wider structures and systems of inequality, which benefit from women's inferior and subordinate status, and therefore sustain them. They operate as part of a system that normalizes and controls rather than just a set of discriminatory beliefs. It is critical for States Parties not only to address their gender stereotypes themselves, but importantly, also the underlying attitudes, systems and structures that give rise to and sustain them. This must entail research, analysis and identification of the root causes giving rise to and sustaining these ideas and practices. In this general recommendation, the term gender stereotypes we use to also refer to prejudices, stigma, bias, and all other beliefs, assumptions, customary, and organizational cultures that shape or contribute to discriminatory social practices. Men and boys are also shaped and impacted by gender stereotypes. Across the world, patriarchal masculinities define ideals of manhood which are not always in men's interests, but which define certain constructs of masculinity that are highly privileged. Most men and boys are socialized to conform to these norms to gain acceptance within the group. They build upon harmful traits, attitudes and behaviours that consistently normalise inequality and encourage violence, discrimination, domination, exploitation, control, militarisation, colonialism and a lack of accountability and care affecting women and girls, but importantly, also men and boys and entire societies. These attitudes justify and establish discriminatory practices in law, custom, and all aspects of social and economic life. Gender stereotypes, prejudices, bias, and stigma are often justified, as we heard earlier, under the banners of tradition, culture, religion, and as my colleague mentioned, so-called family values, and even nature. Discriminatory practices against women and girls need to be eliminated, regardless of their origins, including those perpetuated through misinterpreted notions of culture and religion. After two years of comprehensive work, beginning with a half-day of general discussion in February 2025, briefings to States Parties and other groups, and eight regional and subregional consultations in the Pacific, East and South Asia, West and Central Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, the Caribbean Community, Asia, Europe and Central Asia, and the Arab States, we thank UN Women and all UN agencies that supported this process as we move towards conclusion. The final reading and adoption of GR 41 on dismantling gender stereotypes, prejudices and stigma and the power relations that sustain them. The final reading and adoption will take place during CEDAW's upcoming session in October. And we thank you for being here. and for lending us your ear. Thank you.

Let me introduce myself. I'm Rosina Rossi. I'm a judge in the Uruguayan justice system, have been for 41 years. director of the judicial school centre for judicial studies in Uruguay between 2017 and 2023. Currently, I am in charge of training judges and lawyers in the state as president of the administrative litigation court of Uruguay. I will be sharing an institutional experience related to gender stereotypes and training justice operators to act in cases of gender-based violence in all areas, criminal, civil, labour and in other areas, and in cases of private relations and with the state. In 2019, the interagency gender group of the UN in Uruguay tasked the judiciary school and the attorney general of the nation to develop two practical guides on gender stereotypes and international standards on the rights of women. One of those documents is geared towards justice operators, judges and public defenders within the judicial authority, and the other is aimed at staff in the attorney general's office, which, in Uruguay, lies outside the judicial authority. The draft was also supported by the Spanish Agency for International Cooperation and the OHCHR. branch in Uruguay. Of the two guides, I'll be highlighting the following points: the purpose, the process of drafting, the content, the format of the guides, and I'll be concluding with a brief assessment. So what was the purpose of the guides? The two documents consist of a practical guide but with theoretical support aimed at helping the work of justice operators when they have to act in response to life problems that affect human dignity and gender. The drafting process of those two guides was supported and guided the drafting of the documents, but we should highlight in particular the fact that the operators themselves, who are representatives of judges, public defenders and prosecutors, diagnosed the most common problems facing the Uruguayan community and best profiled how to implement training and the seeking of solutions. The content that the two guides have in common is that they have five main chapters. The first chapter is on general definitions, including what a gender perspective means, the reasons for introducing a gender perspective, what gender-based violence means, international standards and language as a form of perpetuating inequality. Chapter 2 the legal framework of human rights law, which includes both the universal and regional contexts, in our case, the terms of the region, the Americas. Chapter three, the role of justice operators and how to implement in that role the gender perspective. Now, on this point, each guide refers specifically to the respective functions involved. The guide for the judicial authority refers to problems of judicial practice that face judges and public defenders, while the guide for the attorney general refers to those problems inherent to its functioning in the criminal domain. Chapter 4 contains a sort of self-test, a self-test to be carried out by a judiciary operator during each stage involved in his or her action. In other words, in understanding the problem before the justice system, in evaluating evidence and the final decision. Now this self-test's purpose is for the operator to examine his or her own action, ensuring that he doesn't himself become trapped in gender stereotypes that are so deep-rooted in the community. And then there is a set of questions that the operator will put to his or herself and that can be applied to each specific case. Chapter five, then. Chapter five is dedicated to jurisprudence. It's split into two sections, one on cases before the Inter-American Human Rights Court and the CEDAW Committee. It also has a second section, which is a guide on where and how to seek international jurisprudence. That is the content of the two guides. I will now turn to the format. The two guides use simple terms and accessible language. They were edited in paper and digital form. published this by UN Women Latin America and the Caribbean. They are practical, straightforward guides of about 8,000 words in a user-friendly paper format so that, because judiciary operators can have it on their work desk, given that Uruguay, you see, is still the majority of the justice system still uses paper files. Now, turning then to the assessment. So the guides constitute a useful instrument to visualize, understand and resolve cases of discrimination against women that are adapted to universal and regional norms, as well as the recommendations of the CEDAW Committee. They adapt those norms to the specific problems facing the Uruguayan community and its cultural idiosyncrasies. What is particularly valuable is that it was put together by the representatives of the operators themselves, the people who would be using those guides. At the request of the OHCHR office in Uruguay, the guides were later presented in Latin American countries, especially during the first few years after publication. Either way, when carrying out a forward-looking assessment from a human rights perspective in terms of access to justice, it is crucial to understand that the guides are just one step and that, to properly deconstruct gender stereotypes, it is vital to insist on ongoing training of all State operators. those in the justice system, but others also, all state operators who wield power. Therefore, those who act for the state should, or we should, in my condition as a judge, be accountable case by case as to how power is used in the best way to guarantee human dignity. Today, on behalf of the administrative justice system in Uruguay, who specifically is the one that controls the use of the power of the state, I want to thank you.

Thank you, excellencies, distinguished panelists, ladies and gentlemen. At a moment of growing polarization, misogyny, and militarization, we need to understand gender stereotypes for what they do. They organize power. They shape who leads and cares, who protects and who is protected, whose knowledge counts, and whose exercise of power and violence is considered legitimate. Gender stereotypes fuel deepening polarization. They amplify misogyny through the manosphere and normalize militarization, dominance, aggression, and force as answers to security. We see the consequences of this today when these links are ignored. The escalation from stereotype into structural discrimination has been mentioned. From discrimination into institutionalized oppression is the next step. and from cultures of domination into conditions that enable and fuel violence and conflict. Accordingly, states must move from challenging individual stereotypes to addressing and transforming the institutions that reproduce them. There is a responsibility to transform the gendered power relations and institutions that enable discrimination, domination, and violence. From our homes and communities to our economies, political institutions, and systems of peace and security. Across all spheres of society, policies need to ask what assumptions about masculinity, femininity, authority, care, violence, and protection does this institution reproduce? Who benefits and who is excluded? And critically, how is this policy challenging these stereotypes? Transforming harmful gender stereotypes changes how communities distribute productive labor, unpaid care, resources, and power, and will inevitably reduce some of the economic and social conditions through which insecurity and violence are reproduced. The gender impact assessment is already an established governance tool, including across many OECD countries, where the stated policy goal is indeed gender transformative policy that changes gender norms and power relations. So the broad recommendation is that states should integrate this analysis of gender stereotypes, masculinities, and unequal power relations into existing gender impact assessments, gender analysis, and policy review processes. including in security sector reform and governance, peace processes, DDR, arms control policy, national action plans and women, peace and security, and require that identified discriminatory or stereotype reinforcing impacts to result in policy change. Second, militarized masculinities must be part of conflict prevention, human rights investigation and accountability, and this has already been mentioned. We know that a militarised masculinities lens allows us to examine how masculine norms and expectations influence the perpetration of violence, the gender targeting of victims and forms of violence, and the barriers that survivors face in testifying, reporting and seeking services and assistance. Transforming these is critical to break cycles of institutionalised and normalised violence to prevent its recurrence. And without this analysis, we risk holding individuals accountable while leaving the very architecture of violence untouched, which allows militarized notions of domination, force, and masculinity to remain embedded in institutions and reproduce the violations we seek to present. So concrete recommendations, and here I would echo the Deputy Executive Director of UN Women, should include that commissions of inquiry, fact-finding missions, and national early warning systems, transitional justice, and other investigative mechanisms should examine militarized masculinities as structural drivers and enabling conditions of violations, because findings about these can inform accountability and progress guarantees of non-repetition. Third, there is a political economy behind gender stereotypes. WILPF has documented firearms marketing that associates weapons with militarised masculinity, strength and manhood. The gun industry sells not just a product but an identity, and firearms themselves increase women's exposure to serious forms of gender-based violence. Masculinity is monetised by selling weapons, attention or outrage, and this means inequality is fuelled by a business model and personal profit. And this is why WILPF's submission to CEDAW on General Recommendation 41 recommended to recognize the gun industry's exploitation of violent and militarized notions of manhood. It is also why states must incorporate gender stereotype analysis into regulation and human rights due diligence covering firearms, advertising, and marketing, address the partnerships between firearms marketing and digital gaming and entertainment ecosystems, and strengthen corporate accountability for the gendered harms that result. Without accountability for industries that monetise gender stereotypes, from selling weapons through militarised masculinity to profiting from online misogyny, we leave powerful commercial incentives in place to reproduce the very norms of violence that human rights policy seeks to dismantle. Finally, we must treat the prevention of gender stereotyping as part of preventing authoritarianism, violence and conflict. Gender norms that equate masculinity with strength, domination, force and protection, and position women as vulnerable or in need of protection, do not remain in the private sphere. They underpin militarised understandings of security, legitimise violence and shape who holds power, whose authority is recognised and whose security is prioritised. We see this continuum in different forms, from some countries where discriminatory ideas about how women should dress and behave are given legal force and enforced through policing and surveillance, And the most extreme manifestation of this continuum we see in Afghanistan, where gender stereotypes are embedded in the institutionalised framework of gender apartheid, a deliberate system of gender-based discrimination, which is not just an accumulation of individual restrictions, it is gender apartheid and must be named, challenged and met with accountability rather than normalisation. The concrete recommendation to states can and should already recognise this system as gender apartheid, even while efforts to codify it as an international crime through the Crimes Against Humanity Treaty progress, as formally proposed by Australia, Iceland, Mexico, Spain, Timor-Leste and Uruguay. And this should include diplomatic and policy responses that resist the normalisation of the Taliban regime. In conclusion, human rights and transforming harmful gender norms are integral to conflict prevention itself. Addressing discrimination, inequality, misogyny, militarized masculinities, that enable violence before they escalate is critical to protect civic space and those challenging these norms, as well as to integrate gender transformative approaches across human rights monitoring, WPS plans, security sector reform, peace building and disarmament. And finally, to resource feminist movements and community led work with men and boys investing in the rights, care, social infrastructure and nonviolent institutions that build resilient and peaceful societies. Thank you. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished panelists, colleagues. Thank you for the opportunity to contribute to this important discussion. We were glad to see this Council's own framing echoed elsewhere that gender stereotypes are both a root cause and a consequence of discrimination. That is the language used in the CEDAW's ongoing work on General Recommendation No. 41, which has been cited many times today, and to which Play International also made a written submission, arguing for a consistent life cycle, age-responsive approach. It is the same argument that we bring here today, because two mechanisms addressing the same problem should reinforce each other and not produce five different versions of it. At Plan International, we have been looking closely at what it takes to move from recognizing gender stereotypes as harmful to transforming the structures and power relations that allow them to persist. Gender stereotypes do not begin when a woman enters the workplace, stands for election, or becomes a political leader. They begin much earlier. through in childhood, through gender socialization in the family, at school, and increasingly in digital spaces, from cartoons to social media feeds. Age, like gender, is a structural ground of discrimination, and the two compound each other. A girl does not experience stereotyping the same way, at the same moments, or with the same consequences as an adult woman. So the obligation to transform the deeply embedded social and gender norms, expectations, and power relations that produce prejudice cannot stop addressing adults' attitudes. It must reach the point where those norms are firstly learned. They are communicated through what toys and games children are steered towards, what subjects and sports girls are encouraged or discouraged to, what responsibilities they are expected to assume, whose voices are allowed to matter. Small choices in childhood narrow, one by one, into who leads, who earns, and who is heard as an adult. Today, girls resist these norms. Our 2025 research with Cardiff University, titled "Girls' Everyday Resistance," found that most girls in the study practice what we call secret behavioral resistance, challenging norms quietly because challenging them openly can carry real consequences, punishment, violence, stigma, exclusion. It is great that girls are resisting discrimination, that's some progress. But why do they have to resist at all? This is why prevention matters. And prevention is not about persuading individuals. It is about changing the institution and power structures that give a stereotype its authority. These patterns are learned, which means they can also be unlearned and something different can be built in their place. PLANS work through community jambays, brings women, men, people of all genders, young people, religious leaders, community, traditional leaders, authorities together to examine norms and harmful practices, creating space for conversation that are often taboo and engaging men and boys directly in reflecting on power and privilege. And systems have to change too. Plan's Redefine the Rules initiative in Bangladesh works across four dimensions, rights, representation, resources, and reality check, with young people not as beneficiaries, but also as co-creators and co-designers and who hold institutions accountable. This is the shift I will emphasize today, from changing attitudes to expanding agency to transferring power.
